lead: A process is a running program. Linux gives it a PID, a parent PID and a state. The shell runs some processes in the foreground and others in the background. An administrator lists these processes, changes their CPU priority, and ends them with signals. This matters on any shared machine: a stuck browser, a runaway script, or a server job that must keep running after logout. Some syllabi call this process control or job control.
prereq: You need the kernel, shell and command line from Unit 1, and file permissions from Unit 2; account identity is in Chapter 4.2.

blocks.text: A program on disk is passive. When Linux starts it, the kernel creates a process: the running copy with its own memory, open files and identity. Every process has a PID (process identifier), a positive number. It also has a PPID (parent process identifier). The shell that starts a command is the parent; the command is the child. Some processes start other processes, so a tree forms. PID 1 is init, or systemd on modern systems. The kernel starts it directly as the first user-space process, and every other process is created by a parent process, so a tree of PIDs and PPIDs forms below PID 1.

A process state shows what it is doing now. It can be new, ready, running, waiting for I/O, or terminated. Only one process per CPU runs at an instant; the scheduler moves others between ready and waiting. The shell also labels jobs. A foreground job owns the terminal and receives Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Z. A background job is started with &; the shell prompt returns at once and the job runs without owning the terminal, so Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Z do not reach it. The shell prints a job number and PID, as in sleep 300 & giving [1] 4242.

ps takes a snapshot. With no options it shows a short list for your terminal. ps aux shows all processes in BSD style, including USER, PID, %CPU, %MEM, STAT and COMMAND. ps -ef shows UID, PID, PPID, C and full CMD. Use ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd -p PID when you want only named columns for one PID.

What it shows
rows: All processes, user and resource columns

blocks.text: STAT letters: R running or ready, S interruptible sleep, D uninterruptible sleep, T stopped, Z zombie. A sleeping process is normal: it waits for a timer, disk or terminal. top refreshes a live list and sorts by CPU by default. htop is a friendlier viewer with scrolling and kill keys; it may need installation, covered in Chapter 4.3.

A signal is a small message to a process. SIGTERM (15) asks the process to exit cleanly. SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught and ends it at once. SIGINT (2) is sent by Ctrl-C to the foreground job. SIGHUP (1) is sent when a terminal closes; many daemons reload configuration on it. kill -15 PID sends SIGTERM; kill -9 PID sends SIGKILL. killall sleep matches a command name exactly. pkill -f script.sh matches the full command line. pgrep -f script.sh prints matching PIDs without killing.

Job control works in the shell. Ctrl-Z stops the foreground job with SIGTSTP; it does not end it. jobs lists jobs, bg %1 resumes job 1 in the background, and fg %1 brings it to the foreground. nice -n 10 command starts a command with nice value 10. renice -n 5 -p PID changes a running process. The range is -20 (highest CPU priority) to 19 (lowest). A normal user can only raise the nice value of a process (make it lower priority); lowering it, including setting a negative value, needs root. nohup command & ignores SIGHUP, so the job survives logout; output goes to nohup.out by default.
A zombie has finished but its parent has not collected the exit status. An orphan has lost its parent and is adopted by init or systemd. PID 1 is init or systemd; never kill it.

figure.caption: The worked example: sleep 300 & gives job 1 with PID 4242 under shell PID 4100, and ps shows STAT S. The normal first signal is SIGTERM 15; only if PID 4242 is still alive after 5 s does SIGKILL 9 force it, leaving no row.

spec.title: PID 4242 from start to gone
spec.aria: A downward flow for PID 4242: sleep 300 & gives job 1, ps -p 4242 shows PID 4242 PPID 4100 STAT S, kill -TERM 4242 sends SIGTERM 15, the process may show STAT Z briefly, then no row remains; if it is still alive after 5 s, kill -KILL 4242 sends SIGKILL 9 and it ends at once.

examples.question: A student runs sleep 300 &; the shell prints [1] 4242 and the parent shell has PID 4100. Show the output of ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd -p 4242, then terminate the process with SIGTERM and, if it is still alive after 5 s, with SIGKILL. What are PID, PPID and STAT before and after?
steps: 1. The shell starts background job 1 with PID 4242. Its parent shell has PID 4100, so PPID is 4100.
2. The command ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd -p 4242 prints PID 4242, PPID 4100, STAT S, CMD sleep 300.
3. STAT S means interruptible sleep: sleep is waiting on a timer, not using the CPU.

4. kill -TERM 4242 sends SIGTERM 15. A normal sleep process exits. The process dies at once, but it can show STAT Z for a short time until its parent collects the exit status; the shell normally does this so fast that ps -p 4242 prints only the header line, with no data row for 4242.
5. If the process is still alive after 5 s, kill -KILL 4242 sends SIGKILL 9. The process ends at once.
6. After either signal, PID 4242 is gone. PPID 4100 and STAT S no longer exist for that process.
examples.answer: Before: PID 4242, PPID 4100, STAT S. After SIGTERM 15 the process is terminated; it may show STAT Z briefly, then no row remains. If it survived 5 s, SIGKILL 9 removes it.

traps: Sending SIGKILL first is a classic mistake: it skips cleanup and can leave locks or temporary files. Send SIGTERM 15, wait, then SIGKILL 9.
kill alone sends SIGTERM 15, not SIGKILL 9. kill -9 is the forced one.
PID 1 is init or systemd. Killing it can bring down the machine; never do it.
Ctrl-C sends SIGINT 2 to the foreground job only; it does not stop a background job.
STAT S means sleeping, not stopped. Stopped is T; zombie is Z.

quiz.a: PID is the process identifier, a positive number for the process. PPID is the PID of its parent process.

quiz.q: Why is SIGTERM sent before SIGKILL?
quiz.a: SIGTERM 15 lets the process flush files and remove temporary files. SIGKILL 9 cannot be caught, so cleanup may be skipped.

quiz.q: A process has PID 5010, PPID 5000 and STAT S. You run kill -9 5010. State its PID, PPID and STAT after the command.
quiz.a: The process is terminated; it may show STAT Z briefly, then no row remains.

quiz.q: A background job keeps running after Ctrl-C. Explain why.
quiz.a: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT 2 to the foreground job. A background job does not own the terminal's foreground, so it does not get that signal.

quiz.q: Write shell commands to list job 2, resume it in the background, then bring it to the foreground.
quiz.a: jobs %2 lists job 2, bg %2 resumes it in the background, fg %2 brings it to the foreground.
It makes a command ignore SIGHUP 1 so it survives terminal logout; output goes to nohup.out by default.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a zombie and an orphan process?
quiz.a: A zombie has finished but its parent has not collected the exit status. An orphan is still running after its parent has died, and is adopted by init or systemd.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production systems use cgroups and systemd slices to limit CPU and memory per service, so one runaway process cannot starve a host. Container runtimes such as Docker put each process in its own PID namespace; inside it, PID 1 is the container's first process. Tools such as systemd-cgtop, pidstat and perf extend the same ps and top ideas. Search for cgroups v2, PID namespaces and systemd resource control.
